## Abstract

Dwarf galaxies are dark matter-dominated systems that are sensitive to feedback and display bursty star formation histories. This makes them ideal probes of the processes that regulate star formation. This work investigates the timescales of star formation rate (SFR) variability in isolated dwarf galaxies using high-resolution cosmological zoom-in simulations of $50$ dwarf galaxies drawn from the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs and Extended Marvelous Dwarfs simulation suites ( $7.3<$ $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $<9.1$ ). We measure star formation histories in $10$ Myr bins and characterize their variability with power spectral densities (PSDs). At the population level, the PSDs of both disk and non-disk galaxies follow a broken power-law, with a break timescale near $100$ Myr. Individually, our galaxies show both smooth and bursty star formation. A subset of disk galaxies show quasi-periodic SFR oscillations about their mean, which we refer to as cyclic star formation. The dominant timescale of these oscillations scales linearly with half-light radius and is approximated by the orbital period at that radius. Cyclic galaxies have Magellanic Spiral (Sm) morphologies and host lopsided dipole gas disks. In these systems, the bulk of the gas in the lopsided disk moves between its maximum and minimum distance from the galactic center, compressing the star-forming gas once per radial orbit and driving the SFR cycle. Cyclic star formation adds a narrow Lorentzian component to the PSD, peaked at radial orbital frequency of the disk ( $\sim 200-500$ Myr), which is comparable to burst timescales inferred from observations.

## I Introduction

Dwarf galaxies ( $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $<9.5$ ) are dark matter dominated systems with shallow potential wells, which leaves them sensitive to feedback, mergers, and environment [13, 58, 8, 57, 74, 18, e.g.,]. These processes operate on different timescales and leave their imprints on the star formation histories (SFH) that dwarf galaxies display. Disentangling the contribution of each process requires constraining the variability in star formation rates (SFR), and the timescales over which they take place.

Observations find that dwarfs form stars in bursts [88, 56, 55, 101, 46, 7, 6, 60], and constrain that variability through tracers averaging over different timescales [102, e.g.,]. H $\alpha$ and far ultraviolet (FUV) emission trace star formation over $\sim 10$ Myr and $100$ Myr, respectively. [102] and [22] both argue for significant bursts in low-mass galaxies ( $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $\lesssim 9$ ), with burst timescales of $\sim 100$ – $300$ Myr that lengthen with stellar mass. With the advent of JWST there is now also evidence for burstiness on $\sim 100$ Myr timescales in cosmic-noon dwarfs [62] and in typical galaxies at cosmic dawn [52, 23, 17, 78, e.g.]. At a population level, and at a given epoch, galaxies observed at different phases of a burst cycle scatter about the star forming main sequence (MS, $M_{\star}$ –SFR relation), with dwarf galaxies occupying a mass regime where the MS scatter grows [43, e.g.,].

On the theoretical side, the extended regulator model provides a physical framework for this variability [15, 87, 39]. In this model the SFR is set by a gas reservoir that is fed by inflow and drained by star formation and outflows [87]. Fluctuations in SFR due to fluctuations in inflow are damped on short timescales because the gas reservoir averages out fluctuations shorter than its depletion time. This leaves the short-timescale burstiness to processes internal to the galaxy, such as feedback cycles, the formation and destruction of individual molecular clouds, and dynamical disturbances. These short-timescale processes all act on roughly a galactic dynamical time and leave the SFR uncorrelated beyond it. The two families of processes result in a SFH power spectral density (PSD) with three power-law regimes separated by breaks around the galactic dynamical time and at the timescale on which the reservoir responds to inflow. The PSD rises at timescale below the galactic dynamical timescale, is flat between the dynamical timescale and the inflow timescale [40], and steeply rises again above it [87]. The flat regime arises because the two timescales are widely separated, leaving a range over which neither process imprints any structure (white noise). [40] measured the PSDs of SFHs across a wide range of simulations, with different galaxy formation or feedback models, and found them to be well described by broken power-laws, with slopes of $\sim 1$ to $3$ below the dynamical break and a flattening towards longer timescales.

Simulations of dwarf galaxies with different prescriptions for baryonic physics predict bursty star formation in low-mass systems, but differ on the timescales and mechanisms that play a role [85]. In the FIRE-2 simulations, dwarf galaxies ( $7\lesssim$ $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $\lesssim 9.6$ ) form stars in bursts on $\sim 100$ Myr timescales, their cold gas is dispersion dominated, and long lived stellar disks are rare [21, 36, 11]. SFR variability occurs because, after each burst, star forming gas is expelled to larger radii causing a period of relatively low star formation. The gas returns to the central region due to gravitation, triggering the next burst. This causes “breathing modes” [85] that couple the dwarf galaxy’s size to its sSFR [21, 64]. In contrast, the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs (MMD) simulations produce compact galaxies [18], which can grow in size due to secular buildup of stellar mass in angular-momentum supported disks at relatively stable sSFRs [47, 28].

In this work, we examine high spatial and mass resolution cosmological zoom-in simulations of $50$ isolated dwarf galaxies ( $7.3<$ $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $<9.1$ ) from the MMD and Extended Marvelous Dwarfs suites [18]. These galaxies lie in the regime where bursty star formation is expected and where disks begin to form, making them an ideal and timely sample for this study. We apply the PSD framework introduced by [87] to probe SFR timescales and identify their physical causes. In particular, we constrain the overall PSD of our sample as a function of morphology and probe galaxies that display periodic SFR variability. We focus our analysis on timescales below the inflow timescale (fluctuation timescales below $<1$ Gyr), which set the overall SFR variability [15, 87, 39].

This paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the simulations, the SFH and PSD measurements, the basis function expansions, the sample, and the high cadence reruns. Section III presents the PSDs of our simulated galaxy sample, separates bursty from cyclic SFHs, and examines how the dominant timescale scales with galaxy properties. Section IV links periodic star formation to the morphology and orbital dynamics of gas disks. Section V places cyclic PSDs in the context of SFH models and discusses their drivers and observational signatures.

## II Methods

### II.1 Simulations

The Marvelous Massive Dwarfs [18, 47, 74, 68, 28] combined with the Extended Marvelous Dwarf [18] simulations, referred to as “Massive Dwarfs” throughout this paper, are a suite of high resolution cosmological zoom-in simulations of individual dwarf galaxies from the Romulus25 simulation volume [90, $(25\ {\rm Mpc})^{3}$ ,]. The zoom-in simulations are run up to $z=0$ and target isolated star-forming dwarf galaxies spanning $7.0\leq$ $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $\leq 9.1$ at $z=0.1$ . We consider a galaxy isolated if no companion with $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $\geq 10$ resides within $1.5$ Mpc at $z=0.1$ [30].

The zoom-in simulations were carried out with the N-body $+$ SPH code ChaNGa [41, 42, 59], incorporating and expanding on hydrodynamic methods from GASOLINE2 [93, 94]. Within the zoom-in region, the gravitational force softening length is $87$ pc, with initial particle masses of $3.3\times 10^{3}$ $M_{\odot}$ , $994$ $M_{\odot}$ , and $1.8\times 10^{4}$ $M_{\odot}$ for gas, stars, and dark matter, respectively. Full particle data outputs are saved at $\sim$ $300$ Myr cadence. We rerun the last $\sim 1$ Gyr of a subset of galaxies of dynamical interest at higher cadence ( $\sim$ $10$ Myr) which we describe in Section II.5.3 and introduce in Section IV.2. The simulations adopt a Planck 2013 cosmology [69, $\Omega_{m}=0.3086$ , $\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.6914$ , $h=0.67$ , $\sigma_{8}=0.77$ ,].

Star formation occurs stochastically in gas that has cooled below $1000$ K and reached number densities above $0.1\ m_{h}\ {\rm cm}^{-3}$ [16]. The formation probability $p_{*}$ follows a modified Schmidt law [45, 86] scheme in which the molecular hydrogen fraction $X_{{\rm H}_{2}}$ regulates when stars can form [16]:

$$ p_{*}=\frac{m_{\rm g}}{m_{\rm s}}\left(1-{\rm exp}\left[-\frac{c^{*}_{0}X_{{\rm H}_{2}}\Delta t}{t_{\rm ff}}\right]\right), $$

where $c^{*}_{0}=0.1$ is the star formation efficiency, $\Delta t$ ( $\sim 1$ Myr) is the timestep, and $t_{\rm ff}$ is the local free-fall time. In practice, this molecular hydrogen dependence drives star formation into gas well above the density floor ( $n\gtrsim 100\ m_{h}\ {\rm cm}^{-3}$ , where $m_{h}$ is the mass of hydrogen). Cooling follows [16], with metal-line cooling and metal diffusion from [77], and non-equilibrium ${\rm H}_{2}$ chemistry tracked throughout. All stellar masses and SFRs are derived assuming a Kroupa [51] IMF. SN feedback follows the multiphase superbubble model of [48], depositing $10^{51}$ erg per event into a temporarily two-phase medium. Thermal conduction regulates mass flow from the cold to the hot phase via evaporation, with each phase carrying independent mass, energy, and non-equilibrium ionization states, and cooling rates computed separately under pressure equilibrium [48].

The Massive Dwarfs include BH seeding and growth, with a seed mass of $10^{5}$ $M_{\odot}$ , lower than achieved in Romulus25 and set by the resolution of dark matter to properly resolve dynamical orbits. The BHs are seeded according to high-redshift gas conditions (high density and low gas temperature regions, with $n>1.5\times 10^{4}$ cm-3 and $T<2\times 10^{4}$ K), motivated by direct collapse seeding models [104, 72, 73], rather than assuming a constant halo occupation fraction of unity [89, 90, 10]. To suppress fragmentation into stars, BH formation is restricted to gas particles with low metallicity ( $Z<10^{-4}$ ) and low molecular hydrogen fraction ( $X_{\mathrm{H}_{2}}<10^{-4}$ ). Accretion onto BHs uses a boosted Bondi scheme [12], and the associated superbubble feedback [89, 90] follows [48].

Halo finding, centering, and merger tree construction follow the methods described in [28]. Briefly, we use Amiga’s Halo Finder [50, 32, AHF,] to identify halos and bound particles, with galaxy shrinking-sphere centers [71, SSC,] and orientations determined using pynbody 11 1 https://github.com/pynbody/pynbody. Halo masses are defined following [14], as the mass enclosed within a sphere whose mean density equals the redshift dependent virial overdensity derived from the spherical collapse model. Halo merger tree construction and sub-halo tracking across snapshots follows the “voter and graveyard” method [38, 29].

To compare with observational stellar masses derived from photometric measurements, we correct the sum of the star particle masses by applying a factor of $0.6$ to all galaxy stellar masses as described in [63], who show that photometrically inferred stellar masses recover approximately $60\%$ of the total stellar mass in star particles for galaxies in our mass scale. At each snapshot, galaxies are oriented face-on using the angular-momentum (AM) vector of bound gas within $5$ kpc of the center. We measure the galaxy’s half light radius ( $R_{\rm e}$ ) in the Johnson $R$ band in the face-on configuration at each snapshot using pynbody. The full list of simulations before sample selection can be found in Table A1 in Appendix A.

### II.2 Star Formation Rate Measurements

We examine how each galaxy assembled its $z=0$ stellar mass through its SFH. Every star particle in the simulations contains a record of its formation time and initial mass, resulting in a maximum temporal resolution finer ( $\sim 1$ Myr) than our fiducial snapshot resolution ( $\sim 300$ Myr). From these records, we build the SFH of each galaxy’s $z=0$ stellar population by constructing histograms of the formation times weighted by star particle initial mass. Motivated by observational measurements of instantaneous star formation rates (SFRs) derived from H $\alpha$ and FUV emissions [102, 22, e.g.,], we adopt temporal bins of $\Delta t=10$ Myr ( ${\rm SFR}_{10}$ ) and $\Delta t=100$ Myr ( ${\rm SFR}_{100}$ ) respectively. We apply the same time range ( $1.5-13.8$ Gyr) and bins ( $\Delta t$ ) for all galaxies when constructing their SFHs.

Though merger trees allow us to separate in-situ star formation from ex-situ accretion on an individual star particle basis, we consider every star particle in the galaxy at $z=0$ when constructing its SFH. We adopt this definition because observationally inferred SFHs recover the cumulative stellar population with little means of isolating in-situ star formation rates across cosmic time. Furthermore, we note that in practice the difference between aggregate and in-situ SFR for our simulated galaxies is negligible after $\sim 6$ Gyr of cosmic time because mergers that introduce significant new stellar mass decline substantially at later epochs. In particular, after $6$ Gyr of cosmic time, satellites account for only $0.5\%$ of the final stellar mass on average, with a standard deviation of $1\%$ and a maximum of $8\%$ (a single low mass outlier) across the sample.

### II.3 Power Spectral Density Measurements

To quantify the characteristic timescales of SFR variability, we adopt the PSD formalism proposed by [15]. Specifically, we compute the PSD of each galaxy’s log star formation time series [40, which is log-normal,] using the standard discrete Fourier transform, computed via Fast Fourier transform (FFT). The FFT yields the full complex spectrum from which we extract PSDs at each positive frequency ( $f_{k}$ , the $k$ -th frequency component) or corresponding fluctuation timescale ( $\tau_{k}\equiv 1/f_{k}$ ). Throughout this work we use $f_{k}$ exclusively rather than angular frequency ( $\omega_{k}=2\pi f_{k}$ ) to avoid confusion.

In addition to the PSD, we make use of both the amplitude ( $\mathcal{A}_{k}$ ) and power ( $\mathcal{P}_{k}$ ) spectra in quantifying the sizes and significance of oscillations and fluctuations.22 2 For a standard FFT with spacing $\Delta f$ : $\text{PSD}_{k}=\frac{\mathcal{P}_{k}}{\Delta f}=\frac{\mathcal{A}_{k}^{2}}{2\Delta f}$ Writing the time series as $\delta(t)$ , we decompose it into a sum of oscillations:

$$ \delta(t)=\sum_{k}\delta_{k}(t),\qquad\delta_{k}(t)=\mathcal{A}_{k}\cos\left(2\pi f_{k}t+\phi_{k}\right), $$

where $\delta_{k}(t)$ is the contribution of frequency $f_{k}$ , with amplitude $\mathcal{A}_{k}$ and phase $\phi_{k}$ .

Motivated by [40], we adopt Welch’s method [103], which reduces spectral density variance by averaging over overlapping windowed segments. The adopted parameters are listed in Table B2; in particular, setting the segment length equal to the full time series recovers the frequency resolution of the standard FFT while retaining the benefits of windowing and de-trending [35].

### II.4 Basis Function Expansions

In the same way that we use PSDs to characterize the timescales that contribute to a galaxy’s SFH, we use basis function expansions (BFEs) to characterize the spatial structure (i.e., shape) of each galaxy’s stellar and gas distributions. BFEs represent the density and potential fields of a galaxy as a linear combination of orthogonal functions. Specifically, we use the empirical, bi-orthogonal basis function approach of [99] and [66], as implemented in the EXP package and its Python interface pyEXP 33 3 https://github.com/EXP-code/EXP [67]. The expansion coefficients provide a compact summary of the mass distribution. In this work we use the expansions only to quantify how far the stellar and gas disks depart from axisymmetry (Section IV.1). Because the coefficients also describe the potential, the same expansions can be used to compute the radial and azimuthal orbital frequencies of these non-axisymmetric disks directly, which we plan to explore in future work.

#### II.4.1 Cylindrical Basis

In this work, we make use of the cylinder basis of EXP. EXP represents disk densities through defining a rotation from a spherical basis into a user-defined disk density [99, 66]. The resulting basis functions are meridional planes in $R$ and $z$ (‘radial orders’, denoted with $n$ ), multiplied by $e^{im\phi}$ (‘azimuthal order’, denoted $m$ ), weighed by the (complex) coefficients, $C_{mn}$ . We include both vertically symmetric and vertically anti-symmetric terms in our expansion. The lowest-order function represents the target density, such that the azimuthal harmonic $m{=}1$ terms describe a lopsided disk (i.e. dipole), $m{=}2$ terms describe bars or two-armed spirals, et cetera. We adopt as the target density an exponential disk with an isothermal vertical profile [81]:

$$ \rho_{0}(R,z)=\frac{M_{\rm d}}{4\pi a^{2}h}\,\exp\left(-\frac{R}{a}\right){\rm sech}^{2}\left(\frac{z}{h}\right), $$

where $M_{\rm d}$ is the total disk mass, $a$ the scale length, and $h$ the scale height. Equation 3 is not fit to the data. It defines the zeroth-order, equilibrium state of the expansion, and the higher-order terms describe departures from it, such as lopsided or barred disks.

We center each galaxy on its shrinking-sphere center and rotate it face-on using the AM vector of the bound gas within $5$ kpc of the center (Section II.1). We build a separate basis for each galaxy, setting $a$ and $h$ to the stellar half-mass radius and half-mass height. We then compute the coefficients of the stellar and cold gas ( $\log(T/{\rm K})<3.8$ ) components from particles within $20$ kpc of the center, which is a volume that contains the bulk of the disk in every galaxy in our sample. The full cylinder basis parameters are listed in Table B3 in Appendix B.2.

#### II.4.2 Coefficient Powers and Amplitudes

We summarize each expansion by the power in each azimuthal order $m$ , summed over radial order $n$ :

$$ P_{m}=\sum_{n=0}^{n_{\rm max}-1}\left|c_{mn}\right|^{2}, $$

where $c_{mn}$ are the expansion coefficients. We measure deviations from axisymmetry using the amplitude in each harmonic normalized by the axisymmetric amplitude:

$$ \frac{A_{m}}{A_{m=0}}\equiv\left(\frac{P_{m}}{P_{0}}\right)^{1/2}. $$

We report $A_{m=1}/A_{m=0}$ as a measure of lopsidedness (the dipole amplitude). The power in each harmonic is an approximate summary of the expansion, but it is sufficient for the comparisons made in this work.

### II.5 Simulated Galaxy Sample

#### II.5.1 Final Sample

Our simulation suite consists of $53$ galaxies, with $41$ from the Massive Dwarfs and $12$ from the Extended Marvelous Dwarfs suite. All galaxies across both suites share the same simulation setup detailed in Section II.1. We exclude from our final sample two galaxies, r615 and r918, which recently experienced a major merger. We exclude an additional galaxy, r1223, from the analysis as its star formation history was not available. Excluding the three galaxies, the final sample consists of $50$ galaxies with a total mass range of $10.2\leq$ $\log(M/M_{\odot})$ $\leq 11.0$ and stellar mass range of $7.3<$ $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $<9.1$ .

#### II.5.2 Disk Galaxy Classification

We adopt the kinematic disk classification of [18] and [28]. For each galaxy, we compute the circularity parameter $\hat{j}_{z}=j_{z}/|\vec{j}|$ , where $\vec{j}$ is the specific angular momentum of a stellar particle and $j_{z}$ is its component along the $z$ axis. A galaxy is classified as disk-dominated (hereafter a disk galaxy) if the median $\hat{j}_{z}$ of its stellar population exceeds $0.5$ , and as non-disk otherwise. Constructing subsamples of our final sample on this basis, we identify $32$ disk galaxies ( $64\%$ ) and $18$ non-disk galaxies ( $36\%$ ). Both the disk and non-disk sub-samples span the full stellar mass range listed above, both with a mean stellar mass of $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $=8.2$ .

#### II.5.3 High-Cadence Snapshot Reruns

To study the orbital dynamics of our simulated galaxies in detail, we re-simulate the final $\sim 1$ Gyr of $12$ galaxies of dynamical interest from the original suite, saving snapshots at a cadence of $\sim 10$ Myr. Each rerun restarts from the corresponding snapshot of the original simulation and evolves to $z=0$ with the same setup as the original suite (code, resolution, physics, and halo finder). We specifically begin the reruns only $1$ Gyr before $z=0$ to limit the growth of numerical divergence from the “butterfly effect” [49, 31].

## III Power Spectral Density Distributions

Galaxies experience star formation variability (fluctuations) on a range of timescales [15, 87]. In particular, SFR variability occurs on timescales that correspond to the physical processes that govern star formation [see Figure 1 of 40, for a summary of timescales]. In this section, we examine the PSDs of the SFHs of galaxies in our final sample to identify and understand important star formation timescales. First we compare the mean power spectra of the disk and non-disk sub-samples, to see whether morphology affects the distribution of fluctuation power across timescales in Section III.1. In Section III.2 we examine the strength of the periodicity in SFR using the PSDs of individual galaxies. Lastly, we analyze the periods at which the spectra peak and examine how they scale with stellar mass and galaxy size in Section III.3. Throughout this section, although we present the full spectrum, we will focus on physical processes that regulate SFR from $20$ Myr up to $1$ Gyr scales, which correspond to fluctuation timescales up to and including orbital dynamical timescales [54, 44, 87, 40].

### III.1 The PSD of Disks versus Non-Disks

Motivated by [40], we start by examining the Welch PSDs ( ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ ), which averages the Fourier power computed from overlapping segments of a given SFH. This method is ideal for sub-sample comparisons since it suppresses random error on the power at each timescale, which a direct transform may suffer from. The Welch PSDs of individual galaxies in our final sample are computed using the full SFH of each galaxy binned at $10$ Myr intervals (i.e., $\log{\rm SFR_{10}}$ ). Section II.3 gives the details of how we compute ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ .

Figure 1 compares the mean ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ and corresponding 1-sigma spread of the disk and non-disk sub-samples as a function of fluctuation timescale. Both sub-samples show similar PSDs, with broken power-law distributions for timescales below $\tau_{k}<1$ Gyr, followed by an increase in power at longer timescales. To quantify the distribution below $\tau_{k}\leq 1$ Gyr, we use astropy44 4 https://docs.astropy.org/en/v7.1.1/modeling to fit the mean and 1 standard deviation spread of each sub-sample’s distribution within that timescale using a broken power-law model ( $S_{\rm BPL}$ ):

$$ S_{\rm BPL}(f_{k})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}S_{\rm b}\ (f_{k}/f_{b})^{-\beta_{\rm low}}&:f_{k}<f_{b}\\
S_{\rm b}\ (f_{k}/f_{b})^{-\beta_{\rm high}}&:f_{k}>f_{b}\\
\end{array}\right., $$

where $S_{\rm BPL}(f_{k})$ is the PSD value at frequency $f_{k}$ , $f_{b}$ is the break frequency (break timescale is $\tau_{\rm b}\equiv 1/f_{\rm b}$ ), and $S_{\rm b}=S_{\rm BPL}(f_{b})$ is the normalization; ${\beta_{\rm low}}$ is the low frequency slope (longer timescales), while ${\beta_{\rm high}}$ is the high frequency slope (short timescales).

Both sub-samples result in a flat slope on the long timescales ( ${\beta_{\rm low}}<0.01$ ), with a reduced chi squared ( $\chi^{2}_{\nu}$ ) of $1.53$ for disks and $1.96$ for non-disks. On short timescales, the disk results in a slope of ${\beta_{\rm high}}=2.05$ and non-disk sub-samples results in ${\beta_{\rm high}}=2.59$ . The disk galaxy sub-sample results in a slightly higher break timescale ( $\tau_{\rm b}=137$ Myr) than non-disk sub-sample ( $\tau_{\rm b}=91$ Myr). We note that these broken power-law fits indicate that the overall shape of the PSD within $\tau_{k}\leq 1$ Gyr resembles a Lorentzian distribution centered at $f_{k}=0$ (i.e. $S(f_{k})\propto 1/(1+f_{k}^{2})$ ). This distribution, which is also the power spectrum of a damped random walk, is characterized in log-space by Brownian noise ( $\beta=2$ ) on short timescales and white noise ( $\beta=0$ ) on long timescales [15, 40].

The overall average behavior of the MMD measured spectra, regardless of morphology, is in good agreement with both analytic expectations and previous simulation studies. [87] showed (see their Section 3.2 and Appendix C) that star formation sustained by the stochastic formation and disruption of molecular clouds produce a damped random walk ( $\beta_{\rm low}=0,\ \beta_{\rm high}=2$ ). Our break timescales of $\sim 100$ Myr fall within the range of characteristic timescales predicted by their framework. Our spectra also compare well with the PSDs measured by [40] across a large set of cosmological simulations with different galaxy evolution models, including the Marvel suite [2] which use the same code and similar physics to the MMD simulation suite. In particular, the MMDs exhibit similar broken power-law slopes to those measured for the zoom-in simulations with varied galaxy formation models examined in [40] ( $\beta_{\rm low}=0,\ \beta_{\rm high}\approx 1.5\ \text{-}\ 2.5$ ). However there is also interesting information in the individual power spectra of MMD galaxies that show some of them have power at preferred frequencies, which we explore in the next section.

### III.2 Bursty versus Cyclic Star Formation

In Section III.1 we analyzed the overall shape of our PSDs for our disk and non-disk sub-samples over cosmic time. In this section, we examine the variability of SFR against the mean (baseline) SFR for individual galaxies. We consider fluctuations ( $\Delta$ $\log\,\mathrm{SFR}$ ) over the final $4$ Gyr of the simulation. To isolate and measure variability, we subtract out a $1$ Gyr moving average from the $\log{\rm SFR_{10}}$ time series (“mean-subtracted SFR”, $\log\mathrm{SFR}_{10}(t)-\langle\log\mathrm{SFR}_{10}\rangle_{1{\rm Gyr}}(t)$ ). This background subtraction acts as a filter that removes secular evolution of $\log\mathrm{SFR}_{10}$ (e.g., stellar mass of galaxy) and isolates the fluctuations about the slowly varying mean.

While all galaxies in our final sample show similar amplitudes of variability ( $\mathcal{A}_{k}$ , defined in Section II.3) around the mean, a subset of the sources show quasi-periodic behavior (correlated in time, resembling sinusoidal oscillations), with all the periodic variability occurring over a very narrow range of frequency. We will call these systems “cyclic”. We also see galaxies with unstructured strong fluctuations against the mean (uncorrelated in time, resembling white noise), which we will refer to as “bursty”. In their PSDs or amplitude spectra, cyclic galaxies are dominated by a single frequency or timescale while purely bursty galaxies display relatively flat slopes, lacking a favored frequency.

Figure 2 presents the SFH of an example cyclic (r568), bursty (r850), and smooth (r571) galaxy, from top to bottom. The left panel shows the mean-subtracted SFH within the last $4$ Gyr of the simulation. For intuition, we include the corresponding discrete Fourier amplitude spectrum ( $\mathcal{A}_{k}$ ), plotted linearly, in the right panel. The cyclic galaxy ( $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $=9.06$ at $z=0$ ) displays regular, nearly sinusoidal oscillations whose amplitude spectrum is dominated by a single narrow peak at a well defined timescale. In contrast the bursty galaxy ( $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $=7.78$ at $z=0$ ), despite spanning a wider $\Delta\log{\rm SFR}_{10}(t)$ range about the mean than the cyclic galaxy, shows irregular stochastic fluctuations, which results in an amplitude spectrum distributed broadly across timescales and no strongly preferred frequency. We note that not all cyclic galaxies remain cyclic for as long as r568.

Several diagnostics can quantify how cyclic a SFH is relative to its mean. We define a metric based on the power in the sinusoid, $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ , which we call cyclicity. Using the discrete power spectrum of the mean-subtracted SFR, we adopt the ratio of the power in the peak bin ( $\mathcal{P}_{\rm k_{max}}$ ) and its two adjacent bins, which recovers the power leaked out of the peak by the finite time baseline, to the power summed over all frequencies ( $\sum_{k}\mathcal{P}_{k}$ , excluding the DC term $k{=}0$ ) as our definition of the relative $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ of our final sample [24]55 5 Note that, though neither of the following are used in this work, Equation 7 is similar to Fisher’s periodicity test [24], and by the Wiener-Khinchin theorem, $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ tracks the height of the first peak after the first rebound of the autocorrelation function for a sinusoidal signal.:

$$ \zeta_{\rm SFR}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k=k_{\rm max}-1}^{k_{\rm max}+1}\mathcal{P}_{k}}{\displaystyle\sum_{k}\mathcal{P}_{k}} $$

where higher values correspond to more cyclic SFHs. This definition of $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ is convenient in that it is dimensionless and invariant under a rescaling of the SFR $\mathcal{A}_{k}$ . It can be interpreted as the fraction of the total power, or equivalently the fraction of the SFR variance, carried by a dominant frequency. Lastly, for each galaxy in our final sample, we identify the dominant fluctuation timescale ( $\tau_{\rm max}$ ) as the timescale at which the mean-subtracted spectrum peaks ( $\tau_{\rm max}=\tau_{k}(\mathcal{P}_{\rm max})=\tau_{k}(\mathcal{A}_{\rm max})$ ). For reference, the galaxies in Figure 2 have $\zeta_{\rm SFR}=0.68$ (r568), $0.09$ (r850), and $0.11$ (r571).

To probe and benchmark the properties associated with cyclic star formation, we consider galaxies in which the dominant timescale contributes over half of the SFR variance ( $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ $\gtrsim 0.5$ ). We refer to these galaxies as our “most cyclic galaxies” ( $9$ galaxies, $18\%$ of our final sample). Figure 3 shows the normalized ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ of the raw $4$ Gyr SFH (i.e., not the mean-subtracted) of every galaxy in our final sample, split into three bins of $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ . The x-axis is normalized by the timescale of peak ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ power within $\tau_{k}\leq 1$ Gyr. The peak Welch timescale is near the discrete Fourier peak timescale of the mean-subtracted SFH ( $\tau_{\rm peak}({\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch})\approx\tau_{\rm max}$ ). $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ itself is measured separately from the amplitude spectrum of the mean-subtracted SFH (which probes fluctuation against the mean). As $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ increases, the cyclic fluctuations about the mean SFR emerge as a progressively more prominent bump in the raw ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ . Most importantly, we note that the highest values of $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ are occupied by disk galaxies.

Galaxies move in and out of cyclic star formation episodes. The ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ in Figure 3 identifies galaxies that experienced a cyclic phase at some point within the $4$ Gyr window considered in this section (i.e., $\zeta_{\rm SFR}=\zeta_{\rm SFR}^{4{\rm Gyr}}$ ), and the bump is most prominent for those with the strongest and longest episodes. Over the full $13.8$ Gyr window of Figure 1, the same bumps are diluted in power. This is because cyclic star formation only lasts for part of a galaxy’s history, typically at late times, so averaging over the full SFH mixes in long stretches with no cycling. Therefore $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ is also a measure of how significant the cyclic episodes are relative to the SFH window considered. Furthermore, stacking multiple galaxies suppresses the bump further, since $\tau_{\rm max}$ varies from galaxy to galaxy ( $\tau_{\rm max}\sim 200$ – $500$ Myr for $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ $\gtrsim 0.5$ galaxies) and the misaligned peaks average out. In Figure 1, this misalignment appears instead as slightly increased scatter in the stacked ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ on $\tau_{k}\sim 100$ Myr timescales. To understand what sets $\tau_{\rm max}$ for individual galaxies, we analyze the distribution of $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ and $\tau_{\rm max}$ as a function of stellar mass and galaxy size in Section III.3.

## IV Cyclic SFH and Disk Dynamics

In this Section, we link cyclic star formation to galaxy properties to better understand their causes. A size dependence of the dominant SFR fluctuation timescales ( $\tau_{\rm max}\propto R_{\rm e}$ , see Figure 4) is what is expected if cyclic SFR fluctuation timescales are tied to the dynamical timescales of galaxies. In particular, the relation is most apparent for disk galaxies. In this Section, to constrain the relationship between cyclic star formation and disk dynamics, we first explore the morphologies of cyclic galaxies (Section IV.1). We then compare $\tau_{\rm max}$ to the two dynamical timescales of a disk galaxy; the angular orbital period (Section IV.2.1) and the radial period (Section IV.2.2).

### IV.1 Morphologies of Cyclic Galaxies

A key detail associated with galaxies that express the strongest cyclic SFHs is that they are disk galaxies (see Section III.2 and Figure 3). The galaxies in our disk sub-sample feature a wide range of disk morphologies, ranging from classical disks similar to M33 to lopsided disks resembling the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) or NGC 55. On inspection, we find the stellar and gaseous disks of galaxies with the strongest cyclic SFHs are lopsided. These galaxies can be classified as Magellanic Spiral (Sm) or Magellanic irregulars, though not all of them host a bar.

To visualize the differences in morphology, Figure 5 shows the face-on projected density maps of dark matter, gas, stars, and young stars (age $<100$ Myr) at $z=0$ for two galaxies; a stable disk (r571, top row) with a smooth SFH (neither bursty nor cyclic) and a lopsided disk (r568, bottom row) with a cyclic SFH. Both galaxies have similar dark matter ( $\log(M_{\rm dm}/M_{\odot})=10.8$ ) and total gas ( $\log(M_{g}/M_{\odot})=9.7$ ) masses. In r571 the gas and stars are distributed in a symmetric disk, with the young stars tracing the smooth surface density of the gas. In the case of r568, the gas shows an asymmetrical distribution, with the new stars following a similar lopsided distribution.

To quantify the degree to which the stellar and gas disks are lopsided, we use the cylindrical BFEs (Section II.4), applied to the stellar and cold gas ( $\log T/K<3.8$ ) components of the galaxy (see Figure B1 in Appendix B for an example expansion). We use the cold gas because this gas phase traces the star forming component and is largely confined to the galaxy’s disk [28]. Figure 6 shows the normalized dipole amplitude, $A_{m=1}/A_{m=0}$ , of the stellar and cold gas components for each galaxy in the disk sub-sample as a function of $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ . In both components, $A_{m=1}/A_{m=0}$ increases with $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ , with scatter. The most cyclic galaxies ( $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ $\gtrsim 0.5$ ) have systematically larger $m{=}1$ amplitudes in their disks than the less cyclic disks, which indicates increasing lopsidedness.

Comparing the cold gas and stellar lopsidedness, the cold gas shows systematically increasing $A_{m=1}/A_{m=0}$ as a function $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ . This is expected because the cold gas is collisional and responds not only to gravity but also to pressure, feedback, and the angular momentum injected into the disk [28], whereas the stars are collisionless. The stellar disk also includes old stars that formed before the disk settled, so it has a weaker imprint of the disk’s morphology. The cold gas is therefore the component that takes up the shape of the disk and responds on short timescales to perturbations and angular momentum injected during disk formation [28]. This motivates its use as the tracer of disk dynamics and lopsidedness.

### IV.2 Dynamics of Cyclic Galaxies

In this Section we revisit the $\tau_{\rm max}$ – $R_{\rm e}$ relation from Section III.3 and the lopsidedness of cyclic galaxies from Section IV.1 through the lens of disk dynamics. We propose that the periodicity in cyclic SFHs comes from the sloshing of a lopsided disk, which periodically compresses and rarefies the star forming gas relative to its mean density. We explore these connections through relevant dynamical timescales and how they relate to $\tau_{\rm max}$ . We begin with how $\tau_{\rm max}$ scales with idealized angular period and then turn to the radial period of the disk, which sets how often the star-forming gas is compressed.

#### IV.2.1 Angular Orbital Frequencies

To translate $R_{\rm e}$ into an angular dynamical timescale, we approximate the circular orbital period of a parcel of mass in the disk at $R_{\rm e}$ , assuming an axisymmetric mass distribution enclosed within $R_{\rm e}$ , as:

$$ T_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})=\frac{2\pi R_{\rm e}}{V_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})}=\frac{2\pi}{\Omega_{c}(R_{\rm e})}, $$

where $T_{\rm c}$ is the circular orbital time, $V_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})$ the circular velocity determined by the axisymmetric mass enclosed within $R_{\rm e}$ , and $\Omega_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})=V_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})/R_{\rm e}$ is the corresponding circular angular frequency at $R_{\rm e}$ , in radians per unit time.

Figure 7 shows the $\tau_{\rm max}$ -size (left) and $\tau_{\rm max}-T_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})$ (right) distributions for our disk sub-sample, colored by $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ (with red being most cyclic). In the left panel, we show the relation resulting from Equation 8 using the median $V_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})$ of our disk sample ( ${\rm Med}\ V_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})=52~{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ ) and assuming a boundary condition of $\tau_{\rm max}(0)=T_{\rm c}(0)=0$ . This result and the $T_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})$ values of individual galaxies (shown in the right panel) indicate that $\tau_{\rm max}$ is comparable to the angular orbital period at $R_{\rm e}$ .

#### IV.2.2 Radial Oscillation of the Lopsided Gas Disk

In addition to its angular frequency, a lopsided gas disk also oscillates radially, with the off-center overdensity moving inward and outward relative to the galactic center as it completes one orbit. We characterize this motion by its period $T_{\rm r}$ , where $T_{\rm r}$ is the time between successive innermost passages of the bulk cold gas. As stated above, this radial frequency is of particular interest for cyclic star formation because it periodically compresses and rarefies the star-forming gas relative to its mean density. We re-simulate the last $1$ Gyr at high snapshot cadence ( $\sim 10$ Myr) for $11$ of our most cyclic galaxies (ranked by $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ ) and $1$ of our most stable (r571) disk galaxies (see Section II.5.3). Throughout this work we have aligned each galaxy face-on using the AM vector of the corresponding snapshot (Section II.1). In this section we instead use the $z=0$ AM vector as a fixed reference frame so that position angles can be compared across snapshots.

The top row of Figure 8 shows a time series of projected gas density maps for r568 (within $10$ kpc), which has one of the most periodic star formation histories in our sample (see top row of Figure 2 for the SFH and Figure 5 for morphology). Iso-contours of the stellar surface density are overlaid in cyan to show the stellar disk, which remains centered on the galaxy throughout. The second and third rows show mass histograms of the cold gas ( $\log(T/{\rm K})<3.8$ ) in the same galaxy as a function of time, in position angle from the $+x$ axis ( $\theta$ ) and in radius ( $R$ ) from the total-mass shrinking-sphere center, respectively. As mentioned in Section II.1, the shrinking-sphere center is an iterative estimate of the galactic center, obtained by repeatedly computing the center of mass of all particles within a sphere and shrinking its radius until the center of the galaxy’s density peak is identified (i.e., the nucleus of the galaxy, central bulge or bar where one is present). This provides a center that is robust to substructure and to asymmetries in the outer disk. The histogram panels also show an overlay of the $10$ Myr SFR in black for reference, with SFR values on the right axis.

The top row of Figure 8 starts when the bulk of the disk is maximally distant from the center ( $13.43$ Gyr). At this stage, the SFR is near minimum in its cycle (SFR ${}_{10}\sim 0.30\ M_{\odot}\ {\rm yr}^{-1}$ ). Over the following $\sim 0.1$ Gyr the overdensity moves inward, compressing gas near the galactic center, and the SFR rises to a peak at $\sim 13.55$ Gyr (SFR ${}_{10}\sim 0.77\ M_{\odot}\ {\rm yr}^{-1}$ ). The overdensity then moves back outward, the central gas is rarefied, and the SFR falls to a minimum at $13.69$ Gyr. It is important to note that the gas disk is sloshing, not expanding and contracting. The radial change comes from the bulk of the cold gas moving between its furthest and closest approach in the disk. The top row of snapshots show the overall gas morphology does not change dramatically as it oscillates in radial and SFR phase.

The $\theta$ mass distribution in the middle row of Figure 8 shows the lopsided disk’s angular frequency. An important feature to note is that star formation responds to the radial frequency but not necessarily the angular frequency. This is apparent from the two moments of maximum displacement in the first and last panels in the top row of Figure 8 (at $\sim 13.43$ and $\sim 13.65$ Gyr). Both show the cold gas at maximum displacement, but at position angles or apsidal lines that differ. Furthermore, the mass distribution histograms indicate an offset in bulk $\theta$ at each SFR peak.

## V Discussion

In Section III we showed that the stacked ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ of the disk and non-disk sub-samples are similar, both following a broken power law on timescales $\tau_{k}\leq 1$ Gyr with flat slopes on long timescales ( $\beta_{\rm low}<0.01$ ), steep slopes on short timescales ( $\beta_{\rm high}=2.05$ for disks and $2.59$ for non-disks), and break timescales of $\sim 100$ Myr. This shape resembles a damped random walk, in agreement with analytic expectations and previous simulation studies [87, 40]. The power spectra of individual galaxies, however, reveal that a subset of our sample has quasi-periodic (cyclic) SFHs dominated by a single timescale, $\tau_{\rm max}$ . We quantified this behavior with the cyclicity parameter, $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ , defined as the fraction of SFR variance carried by the dominant frequency. The most cyclic galaxies ( $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ $\gtrsim 0.5$ ; $18\%$ of our sample) are exclusively disks with $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $>8.3$ and are not necessarily the burstiest systems. For disks, $\tau_{\rm max}$ scales linearly with $R_{\rm e}$ , pointing to a link between cyclic star formation and disk dynamics.

In Section IV we examined the link between disk dynamics and star formation. The most cyclic galaxies host lopsided stellar and gas disks resembling Magellanic-type irregulars, with the cold gas showing systematically stronger $m{=}1$ asymmetry ( $A_{m=1}/A_{m=0}$ ) than the stars. Across the disk sub-sample, $\tau_{\rm max}$ is comparable to the circular orbital period at the effective radius, $T_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})$ . Using high-cadence reruns of our most cyclic galaxies, we showed that the lopsided cold gas disk sloshes about the galactic center as the bulk of the gas moves between its maximum and minimum radius in its orbit. Star formation peaks when the gas is compressed near the galactic center and declines as it moves outward and is rarefied. This causes the offset of the cold gas center of mass from the galactic center to oscillate roughly in anti-phase with the SFR. The dominant SFH timescale in these systems is therefore set by the radial oscillation period of the gas ( $\tau_{\rm max}\approx T_{\rm r}$ ), which is close to the azimuthal period ( $T_{\rm r}/T_{\rm c}\sim 1$ ). In this section, we discuss the implications of these results and observational signatures of cyclic star formation.

### V.1 The Power Spectra of Cyclic Dwarfs

#### V.1.1 Shape of Cyclic PSDs

The overall shape of the PSDs of cyclic galaxies can be modeled by adding a Lorentzian component centered at orbital timescale to the broken power-law continuum. In particular, the bump or quasi-periodic peak of cyclic galaxies, which spans a small range of frequencies, can be described by narrow Lorentzian component ( $S_{\rm c}$ ):

$$ S_{\rm c}(f_{k})=\frac{S_{0}\ (\gamma/2)^{2}}{(f_{k}-f_{c})^{2}+(\gamma/2)^{2}}, $$

where $S_{0}$ is the peak amplitude, $f_{c}$ the center frequency or offset, and $\gamma$ the full width at half maximum. Because the cyclic star formation in our most cyclic galaxies is a consequence of gas disk orbital dynamics, the $S_{\rm c}$ component is centered near the full orbital time of gas disk (see Section IV.2):

$$ f_{c}=\frac{1}{\tau_{\rm max}}\approx\frac{1}{T_{\rm r}}\sim\frac{1}{T_{c}(R_{e})}. $$

To illustrate the two-component nature of cyclic PSDs, in Figure 11 we stack the normalized ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ of our simulated galaxies, binned by cyclicity, over the last $4$ Gyr of their respective SFHs and fit the resulting mean spectrum with $S_{\rm BPL}(f_{k})+S_{\rm c}(f_{k})$ using astropy. Each PSD is normalized by its peak power and peak timescale $\tau_{\rm peak}\sim\tau_{\rm max}$ prior to stacking, which aligns the cyclic bumps at $\tau_{k}/\tau_{\rm peak}=1$ . The two-component model reproduces both the continuum and the quasi-periodic peak. Therefore the cyclic SFH can be understood as a Lorentzian in the PSD ( $S_{\rm c}(f_{k})$ ) driven by the orbital dynamics of the galaxy’s gas disk. In principle, the continuum break $\tau_{b}$ and the cycle timescale $\tau_{\rm max}$ are free to differ. A broken power-law only fit does not account for the quasi-periodic peak, so the break may be dragged toward $\tau_{\rm max}$ and $\tau_{\rm max}$ could be misread as the break timescale of the cyclic galaxy. This would conflate two physically different timescales, where $\tau_{b}$ reflects the transition to timescales dominated by stochastic formation and disruption of giant molecular clouds [87, GMC,], while $\tau_{\rm max}$ reflects the orbital dynamics of the star forming gas disk. Further detailed exploration of the functional form of cyclic PSDs is left for future work.

#### V.1.2 Cyclic PSDs in the Context of SFH Models

Cyclic SFHs can be placed in the context of two common statistical descriptions of SFH variability, damped random walks and stochastically driven damped harmonic oscillators. The extended regulator model [15, 87, 39] describes the SFH as a sum of damped random walks corresponding to gas inflow, gas cycling, and GMC formation and destruction ( $\leq 1$ Gyr). These processes contribute to a Lorentzian, or a product of Lorentzians, centered at zero frequency ( $f_{c}=0$ ). The sum of these components produce a broken power-law like continuum at $\leq 1$ Gyr timescales. The cyclic bump in particular requires a component peaked at nonzero frequency, which lies outside the family of damped random walks considered by the extended regulator model [39]. Though the bump is well described by the stochastically driven, damped simple harmonic oscillator (SHO) kernel of [25], a single SHO term is not sufficient on its own. Thus, the PSDs of our simulated galaxies are well described by the regulator model, with cyclic galaxies requiring an additional Lorentzian component (Equation 9), driven by the orbital dynamics of the gas disk and centered at radial frequency of their star forming gas disks.

### V.2 What Causes Cyclic Behavior?

Our analysis in Section IV shows that cyclic star formation in dwarf galaxies results from a coupling between the SFR and the dynamics of the star forming gas disk. Cyclic episodes occupy only part of the SFHs of the galaxies that express them, usually at late times for galaxies in our mass range. In the simulations, we often see external dynamical perturbations from merging, companion, or splashback satellites occur around the onset of cyclic behavior [97, 98, 84, 82, 83]. Close encounters with these satellites, typically with $\log(M_{\rm halo}/{\rm M}_{\odot})\gtrsim 8$ , can perturb classical disks onto more eccentric orbits and trigger cyclic star formation, and in some cases a close fly-by or an interaction with a more massive satellite briefly suppresses an ongoing episode. The nature of these interactions varies enough from galaxy to galaxy, that more work is needed to isolate which aspects of an interaction matter most for triggering cyclic behavior. We defer a detailed study of these triggers to future work.

Beyond triggering cyclic SFH, why cyclic episodes can persist for multiple orbital periods is of particular interest as well. Stellar feedback is one possibility that could play a role in allowing the episodes to persist. Each cycle compresses the gas and drives a burst, and each burst contributes feedback. In a shallow potential, this feedback may suppress circularization of the gas, which may lead to feedback coupling that leads to prolonged sustained cyclic star forming episodes (i.e., prolonged sloshing modes).

Another dynamical trigger, and a possible cause of persistence, is an instability in the distribution function, most likely of the dark matter. [100] shows that features in the halo density profile can produce an inflection in the distribution function, so that it no longer satisfies Antonov’s stability criterion [1, $df/dE<0$ , ] and becomes unstable to an $l{=}1$ mode. [20] show that such an inflection develops in ideal spherically symmetric systems whose density profile turns over quickly from a steep outer slope to a shallow inner one. The resulting $l{=}1$ mode in the dark matter halo acts on the disk as a precessing dipole [100], which could produce and sustain the lopsided gas disks of our most cyclic galaxies. Lastly, numerical effects may play a role in the lifetimes of cyclic SFR episodes, though the triggers are physically identifiable. In a follow up work, we will test these possible drivers by examining disk dynamics, star forming regions, and dark matter morphologies in detail. We will also explore the galaxy mass ranges that are most susceptible.

### V.3 Observational Signatures

In this section we discuss possible observational signatures of galaxies that express cyclic star formation episodes. Since the most cyclic galaxies are disk galaxies, a morphological sample selection is needed to filter out non-disk galaxies. One possible approach is to take advantage of the relatively compact sizes of non-disk galaxies and apply a $R_{e}>2$ kpc cut for $8.5<$ $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $<9.5$ (or similar filter accounting for mass–size). This negates the need for morphological classification at the expense of filtering out compact gas disks that may be cyclic.

#### V.3.1 Offset Gas Disks

The most direct signature of a cyclic galaxy is a star forming gas disk whose center does not coincide with the photometric or kinematic center of the stellar body. In our mass range the stellar disk is still building its mass at late times [28], and a significant fraction of the stellar light may lie in the older stellar population that does not share the gas orbit, so the $m{=}1$ distortion is expressed most strongly in the gas or possibly H $\alpha$ regions. We expect the offset to be measurable in $21$ cm maps against the galaxy’s optical isophotal center, and for the ${\rm H}_{\rm I}$ distribution to appear as an $m{=}1$ term in an azimuthal harmonic decomposition [26, e.g., using Fourier-Laguerre basis expansions,]. It is possible to detect the $m{=}1$ mode in stellar disks that have had sustained long cyclic episodes, which builds up a stellar population that inherits the cold gas disk’s kinematics. Regardless of the component considered, measuring the offset requires a sizable sample of dwarf disk galaxies viewed close to face-on or with mild inclinations. It is also possible to detect lopsidedness in edge-on systems whenever the orbital semi-major axis of the gas is close to perpendicular to the line of sight (NGC 55 for example). We expect the most common contaminants to be systems actively undergoing a major merger that have not yet coalesced, which can appear extended and lopsided, often alongside elevated $\log\,\mathrm{sSFR}$ . Since our final sample consists of isolated galaxies, an isolation criterion is also needed to restrict environmental effects.

#### V.3.2 Star Forming Regions

The last column of Figure 5 shows the young stellar population (age $<100$ Myr) for a stable (smooth SFR) and lopsided (cyclic) galaxy. Dwarf galaxies with stable disks in our simulated sample have their star forming regions distributed across the disk. In contrast, strongly lopsided disks undergoing large-amplitude cyclic SFR episodes have concentrated star-forming regions near the center. The compression that triggers a burst in lopsided disks occurs when the bulk of the star-forming gas makes its closest approach to the nucleus (see Figure 8). At peak SFR the star-forming region therefore lies slightly offset from the isophotal center of the continuum (offset H $\alpha$ regions). At the SFR trough, the star-forming gas is at its maximum distance from the nucleus and is spread over the disk, so the H $\alpha$ is diffuse. These trends are observed in galaxies from cosmic noon to the present [105, 33, 75, 76, 53, 61, 80, 79, e.g.,]. For example, Mintz et al. [61] measure nonparametric morphological statistics (Gini, $M_{20}$ , and asymmetry) of both the stellar continuum and the H $\alpha$ emission for dwarfs at $8\lesssim\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})\lesssim 9$ in the Merian Survey [19]. They find that the lowest-mass galaxies with the highest sSFR have H $\alpha$ emission that is compact and slightly offset from the center of the continuum.

#### V.3.3 The 0.2 Gyr Timescale

Because observations capture real dwarf galaxies at a single moment in their star forming cycle, the cycle of any one galaxy cannot be followed. The timescales are instead inferred statistically from ensembles of galaxies observed at all phases, and the scatter in star formation indicators that probe different timescales, such as H $\alpha$ and FUV, constrains the burst amplitude and duration. This allows us to compare simulated star formation timescales to the corresponding timescales inferred from observations. Building on Weisz et al. [102], Emami et al. [22] fit the H $\alpha$ and FUV luminosities of Local Volume galaxies with bursts that rise and decline exponentially and find e-folding times that increase with mass, from $\tau\approx 100$ Myr at $8<$ $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $<8.5$ to $\tau\gtrsim 300$ Myr at $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $>8.5$ . These timescales are of the same order as our simulated final sample (see Figure 4).

At cosmic noon, [62] use a continuum selected sample of $43$ JWST PRISM spectra of low-mass galaxies ( $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $<9.5$ ) and find numerous strong Balmer breaks that anticorrelate with H $\alpha$ equivalent width. Modeling the population with periodic bursts, they constrain burst timescales of $\sim 200$ Myr. The prevalence of long-timescales of burst may be related in some part to cyclic star formation. If the mechanism that stimulates cyclic star formation needs only a gas disk and a perturber, sloshing disks and cyclic episodes could be more common among dwarfs at higher redshifts. Nevertheless, establishing predictions for possible cyclic episodes and their physical mechanism at high redshifts requires further work focused on low-mass systems and their environments in the early universe.

For disk dwarf galaxies, $\tau_{\rm max}$ scaling with $R_{\rm e}$ raises an interesting prediction (see Figure 7). For a disk at the compact/extended boundary of [28], $R_{\rm e}=2$ kpc, and a typical $V_{c}(R_{\rm e})\sim 50\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ for our disk sample:

$$ \tau_{\rm max}\sim T_{c}=\frac{2\pi\,(2\ {\rm kpc})}{50\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}}=0.25\,{\rm Gyr}, $$

which is similar to the periods recovered by H $\alpha$ /FUV analyses. However, a definitive observational test of $\tau_{\rm max}$ scaling with $R_{\rm e}$ requires a sample of dwarf disk galaxies at fixed mass. Dividing these disks into size bins of $R_{\rm e}$ and repeating the H $\alpha$ /FUV fit in each bin would yield a burst timescale per size bin. If the timescale is set by the orbital period, it should grow with $R_{\rm e}$ across the bins, whereas if it is set by mass alone the bins should return the same value. The test does not require separating lopsided disks from stable ones. A lopsided disk raises the amplitude of the variation at $\tau_{\rm max}$ but does not change $\tau_{\rm max}$ itself, so every disk in the sample contributes to the measurement. We expect the clearest trend in the bins with $R_{\rm e}>2$ kpc, since nearly every dwarf above this size in our simulated $z=0$ sample is an angular momentum supported disk [28].

## VI Summary and Conclusions

In this work we measure the timescales of SFR variability in $50$ isolated dwarf galaxies from the Massive Dwarfs simulations ( $7.3<$ $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $<9.1$ ) and link periodic star formation to the dynamics of their gas disks. The key findings of this work are summarized below.

- 1. At the population level, the stacked ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ of both the disk and non-disk sub-samples follow a broken power law on timescales $\tau_{k}\leq 1$ Gyr, flat on long timescales and steep ( $\beta_{\rm high}\approx 2$ – $2.6$ ) on short timescales, with a break near $100$ Myr. This is the shape of a damped random walk and agrees with analytic expectations and previous simulations [87, 40] (see Figure 1 and Section III.1).

- 2. Individually, galaxies show smooth, bursty, and cyclic SFHs (see Figure 2). We quantify cyclic star formation with $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ , the fraction of SFR variance from the dominant frequency (Equation 7). The most cyclic galaxies ( $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ $\gtrsim 0.5$ , $18\%$ of the sample) are exclusively disks with $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})$ $>8.3$ and are not necessarily the burstiest galaxies (see Figures 3 and 4, and Section III.2).

- 3. For disk galaxies, the dominant fluctuation timescale $\tau_{\rm max}$ scales linearly with $R_{\rm e}$ and is approximated by the circular orbital period at that radius, $T_{\rm c}(R_{\rm e})$ (see Figure 7 and Sections III.3 and IV.2.1).

- 4. The most cyclic galaxies host lopsided, Magellanic-type stellar and gas disks. The $m{=}1$ amplitude increases with $\zeta_{\rm SFR}$ and is systematically larger in the cold gas than in the stars (see Figures 5 and 6, and Section IV.1).

- 5. In lopsided galaxies, the lopsided cold gas disk sloshes about the galactic center. Star formation peaks when the bulk of the gas is compressed near the center and declines as it moves outward, so the cold gas COM offset oscillates radially in anti-phase with the SFR and $\tau_{\rm max}\approx T_{\rm r}\approx T_{\rm c}$ . An axisymmetric disk shows no such coupling (see Figures 8, 9, and 10, and Section IV.2.2).

- 6. The PSD of a cyclic galaxy is described by the broken power-law continuum plus a narrow Lorentzian centered at the orbital frequency of the gas disk (Equation 9, see Figure 11 and Sections V.1.1 and V.1.2).

Looking ahead, a follow-up study will use the basis function expansions introduced here to follow the orbits of the star-forming gas directly, identify the perturbations that set lopsided disks in motion, and determine why cyclic episodes persist for several orbital periods. The observational tests above can be carried out with existing H $\alpha$ , FUV, and ${\rm H}_{\rm I}$ surveys of nearby dwarfs, and would establish whether the cycles we find in simulations are present in real galaxies.

## Appendix B Parameters Used in Analysis

### B.1 Welch PSD Parameters

Motivated by [40], we also adopt Welch’s method66 6 Implemented in scipy.signal.welch [103] which reduces spectral variance by averaging over overlapping windowed segments. Welch’s method [103] divides a time series into $K$ overlapping segments, detrends and windows each one, and averages their periodograms. Averaging reduces the variance of the PSD at each frequency, at the cost of frequency resolution, since the frequency spacing is set by the segment length ( $\Delta f=1/(n_{\rm seg}\Delta t)$ ). We set the segment length equal to the full time series ( $n_{\rm seg}=N$ , $K=1$ ), so our ${\rm PSD}_{\rm Welch}$ is a single windowed and detrended periodogram at the finest frequency resolution the data allow. We make this choice because the peaks of cyclic SFHs are narrow. With a single segment the overlap parameter has no effect, and we instead reduce the variance of the PSD by averaging over galaxies when stacking the spectra of a sub-sample. The Hann window tapers the series smoothly to zero at both ends, which suppresses leakage of power from the strongly populated low frequencies into high frequencies. For spectra like ours, this leakage would otherwise flatten the measured high-frequency slope. Table B2 summarizes the adopted parameters.
